4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation

A bank's customer-service agents will keep their roles but need to learn to work with an AI assistant. Some data-entry roles will largely disappear, and those employees will be trained for new roles as AI quality reviewers. Which terms describe these two workforce actions?
Reskilling for the agents; upskilling for the data-entry staff
Upskilling for the agents; reskilling for the data-entry staff
Upskilling builds new skills for an existing role, such as agents working with AI.
Reskilling prepares people for a different role, such as data-entry staff moving to AI quality review. Option A reverses the terms, and offboarding and outsourcing aren't what's described.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
A company is designing an AI literacy program for 8,000 employees. Which approach is most effective?
The same three-day technical course for everyone
Role-based learning paths: baseline AI literacy and responsible use for all staff, strategy and risk for leaders, and deeper skills for builders and power users
A one-hour video with no follow-up

Everyone needs basic literacy and safe-use rules, leaders need to understand strategy, value, and risk, and builders need technical depth. One-size-fits-all courses waste time, training only specialists leaves most users unprepared, and a single video doesn't build lasting skills.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation

An IT team built an AI scheduling tool for field technicians without talking to them. At launch, technicians found it ignored real constraints such as traffic patterns and parts availability, and adoption collapsed. What would have prevented this?
Involving end users early in discovery, design, and pilot testing so the solution fits their real workflow
Adoption depends on fit with real work.

Involving users early surfaces constraints, builds ownership, and creates champions. Launch events, more advanced models, and mandates don't fix a solution that doesn't match how the work is actually done.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
A company will roll out generative AI tools to all employees over six months. What should its communication plan emphasize?
A single announcement on launch day only
Regular, honest, audience-specific updates: why the change is happening, what it means for each group, how support works, and how feedback is being used
Technical details of the model architecture for all staff
Effective change communication is repeated, honest, and tailored.

It explains the "why," what's in it for each audience, and the support available, and it shows that feedback matters. One-time announcements, leadership-only updates, and deep technical detail don't drive adoption.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation

Which TWO practices reflect effective change management for AI adoption? Pick the pair of correct statements.  (1) Start change management in the week of launch.  (2) Plan change management from the start of the initiative, alongside the technical work.  (3) Measure success only by whether the technology was deployed.  (4) Treat change management as optional for "simple" AI tools.  (5) Track adoption and user sentiment and use them to adjust training and support.
Change management should start early and be measured through adoption and sentiment metrics, then adjusted as needed.
Starting at launch is too late, deployment alone isn't success, and even simple tools need people to change how they work.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
A logistics company is staffing the team for its first production AI initiative, an AI-assisted freight quoting tool. Which team composition is most likely to succeed?
A cross-functional team: a business product owner, the sales users who will use the tool, data and technical specialists, and legal and risk advisors as needed
An external vendor working with no internal involvement
AI initiatives succeed when business, user, data, technical, and risk perspectives work together from the start.
Single-discipline teams miss either business fit or technical feasibility, and fully outsourced work leaves the company without internal ownership.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
In an AI initiative, who should play the product owner role, and what's its main responsibility?
A business leader accountable for the AI product's business value, who prioritizes features and decides trade-offs based on user and business outcomes
The vendor's account manager, who maximizes license sales
The newest team member, who takes meeting notes
The infrastructure engineer, who chooses server sizes
A product owner from the business keeps the AI work tied to outcomes, prioritizes the backlog, and makes value trade-offs.
Vendors have their own incentives, note-taking isn't ownership, and infrastructure sizing is a technical task.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
Three months after buying 2,000 licenses for an AI assistant, usage data shows only 400 people use it weekly. What's the most effective next step?
Buy 2,000 more licenses to increase visibility
Assume the other 1,600 will start eventually
Investigate the barriers through user interviews and usage analysis, then offer targeted enablement such as role-specific use cases, training, and workflow integration
Low adoption is a signal to diagnose, not to ignore or overreact to.

Common causes are unclear use cases, lack of skills, poor workflow fit, or trust concerns, and each needs a targeted fix. Cancelling too early wastes the investment, buying more licenses adds cost, and waiting rarely changes behavior.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
A successful pilot of an AI claims assistant in one region is approved for scaling to 12 regions. Which rollout approach best manages risk?
Launch in all 12 regions on the same day
A phased rollout, adding regions in waves and using each wave's lessons, metrics, and feedback to adjust before the next
Roll out only to the CEO's region forever
Restart from a new proof of concept in each region
Phased rollouts limit the damage if issues arise and allow learning and adjustment between waves.
Big-bang launches magnify problems, staying in one region forever gives up value, and repeating proofs of concept wastes proven work.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
A pilot AI tool ran well for 50 users on a team-managed setup with no formal support. Leadership wants it available to 5,000 employees next month. What must be addressed before scaling?
Production readiness: security review, access controls, monitoring and alerting, support processes, service levels, cost controls, and scalability testing

Scaling 100 times exposes gaps in security, reliability, support, and cost that a small pilot hides. Interface colors and names don't affect readiness, and assuming the pilot setup will hold invites outages and incidents.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation

A bank's AI team notices each new generative AI use case takes four months, mostly because it rebuilds data connectors, guardrails, and evaluation tests from scratch. What would most speed up scaling?
A shared AI platform of reusable components, such as approved model access, guardrail configurations, prompt templates, connectors, and evaluation pipelines
Hiring more people to rebuild the same components faster
Skipping guardrails and evaluation for new use cases
Limiting the bank to one AI use case
Reusable platforms lower the cost and time of each new use case and keep governance consistent.
More people rebuilding the same things doesn't scale, skipping safeguards creates risk, and capping the number of use cases limits value.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
A large company wants AI expertise and standards set centrally, while business units build and own their own use cases close to their customers. Which operating model is this?
Hub-and-spoke (federated), with a central hub setting standards and platforms and embedded spoke teams delivering in the business units
Hub-and-spoke combines central consistency (standards, platforms, governance, expertise) with local speed and business ownership.
Fully centralized models often become bottlenecks, fully decentralized ones duplicate effort and create inconsistent risk, and outsourcing gives up ownership.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
A program director proposes building a full enterprise AI solution over 18 months and launching it all at once. What approach does the AI strategist recommend instead?
Make the 18-month plan 36 months to be safe
An iterative approach: deliver in short cycles of usable increments, measure outcomes, gather feedback, and adjust
Wait for AI technology to stop changing
Launch a minimal version with no measurement
Iterative delivery reduces risk, delivers value sooner, and adapts to fast-moving technology and user feedback.
Longer big-bang plans raise the risk of building the wrong thing, waiting for stability never ends, and launching without measurement prevents learning.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation

A generative AI document assistant cost $3,000 a month during its pilot. Scaling to the whole company will raise volume about 50 times, which would cost $150,000 a month at current per-request costs and erase the business case. What should the team do?
Scale anyway and hope prices fall

Revisit unit economics before scaling: right-size the model per task, optimize prompts and retrieval to cut tokens, use batch processing where possible, and consider committed or provisioned capacity for steady volume
Reduce the number of users allowed after scaling
Costs that are tolerable in a pilot can break at scale.

Cost optimization levers often cut unit costs dramatically: smaller models, token efficiency, batch processing, and pricing commitments. Cancelling gives up value, hoping for price drops isn't a plan, and restricting users undermines the reason for scaling.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation

Which TWO conditions should be in place before an AI pilot is approved to scale? Pick the pair of correct statements.  (1) The pilot met its pre-agreed success criteria for value and adoption.  (2) The vendor offered a discount for buying more licenses.  (3) One executive personally likes the tool.  (4) Production support, monitoring, governance, and budget for the scaled solution are ready.  (5) A competitor announced a similar tool.
The decision to scale should rest on evidence (the criteria were met) and readiness (operations, governance, and funding are in place).
Discounts, personal preference, and competitor announcements aren't sound reasons to scale.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation

A conglomerate's eight business units each picked their own AI vendors, guardrails, and data practices. Leadership now finds duplicate contracts, inconsistent risk controls, and no way to share successful solutions. What's the core issue?
A fully decentralized approach with no shared standards, platforms, or governance, which causes duplication and inconsistent risk
The business units are too small
Fully decentralized AI adoption gives speed at first but leads to duplicated spending, uneven risk controls, and lost reuse.
A federated model with shared standards and platforms fixes this while keeping local ownership. The problem isn't too much control, too few tools, or unit size.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
A US retailer's AI product-recommendation engine succeeded domestically. The company wants to scale it to the EU and Japan next quarter. Beyond technical deployment, what must be reassessed?
Nothing, because the model already works
Regulatory and privacy requirements, data residency, consent mechanisms, language and cultural fit, local success metrics, and whether training data represents the new customers
Scaling across borders brings new laws (such as GDPR and the EU AI Act), new data residency and consent needs, language and cultural differences, and customer data the model wasn't trained on.
Each of these can affect compliance, fairness, and performance. Currency and capacity are only part of the picture.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
What's the main purpose of an AI Center of Excellence (CoE)?
To set standards, share best practices and reusable assets, build skills, and help business teams adopt AI faster and more safely
To personally approve and build every AI project in the company
To replace all business-unit decision-making about AI
To manage the office's IT hardware
An AI CoE speeds up and standardizes adoption through expertise, guidance, enablement, and reusable assets.
It shouldn't become the only gatekeeper or builder, take over business ownership, or handle unrelated IT tasks.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation

Two years in, a company's AI CoE has a nine-month backlog because every AI request must be built by the CoE's eight people. Business units are frustrated and some are going around it. What change makes sense?
Disband the CoE and let everyone do whatever they want
Shift the CoE toward enablement: provide platforms, guardrails, templates, and training so business teams can build within standards, with the CoE focusing on complex or high-risk work
Require that all requests wait in line regardless of value
As maturity grows, CoEs should move from doing everything to enabling others through self-service platforms and standards, which scales capacity without losing governance.
Disbanding loses standards, and longer backlogs or rigid queues worsen the bottleneck and encourage shadow AI.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation

An AI customer-service assistant met its targets at launch. A year later, satisfaction has slowly declined because products, policies, and customer questions changed while the assistant didn't. What practice was missing?
Continuous improvement: regularly reviewing performance metrics and user feedback, updating content, prompts, and models, and measuring the results
AI programs are never "done." Continuous improvement loops keep solutions aligned with changing products, policies, and users.
Launch budgets don't sustain value, a single survey is a snapshot, and yearly replacement is costly and unnecessary.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation
The board asks the Chief AI Officer for a quarterly view of whether the enterprise AI program is working. Which set of program-level metrics is most appropriate?
The number of AI-related meetings held
The number of AI vendors contacted
Total GPU hours consumed, with no other context
Business value delivered against targets, use cases in production, adoption rates, risk and incident trends, and progress on capabilities such as skills and data readiness
Boards need outcome-focused metrics that cover value, scale, adoption, risk, and capability building.
Activity counts such as meetings and vendors contacted, or raw usage without context, don't show whether the program is creating value responsibly.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation

A company finds that teams in different divisions keep making the same mistakes on AI projects: underestimating data cleanup, skipping baselines, and launching without change plans. What practice would help most?
Systematic knowledge sharing: a lessons-learned repository, reusable playbooks, communities of practice, and post-project reviews, often coordinated by the CoE
Keeping each project's lessons confidential within its own team
Blaming the teams that made mistakes
Organizational learning turns individual project experience into shared playbooks and patterns, reducing repeated mistakes and speeding up delivery.
Secrecy and blame discourage learning, and stopping projects gives up value.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation

A company's innovation funnel shows that out of 120 AI ideas submitted last year, 30 became proofs of concept, 10 became pilots, and 4 scaled to production with measurable value. How should leadership read this?
The program has failed because most ideas didn't scale
Only 4 ideas should have been submitted
A healthy funnel: many ideas, disciplined filtering, and early stopping of weak ones, with resources concentrated on proven winners
Every idea should have been scaled to production
A healthy AI portfolio deliberately stops most ideas early and cheaply, and puts investment into the few that prove value.
That's disciplined portfolio management, not failure. Limiting submissions reduces options, and scaling everything wastes resources on weak use cases.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation

After a successful AI launch, the project team was disbanded and no one was assigned to the solution. Eighteen months later, usage and value have quietly eroded. What does sustaining AI value require?
A new launch event every year
Ongoing ownership after launch: an accountable business owner, operational support, monitoring of value metrics, and continued reinforcement with users
Removing the solution's metrics so the decline isn't visible
Value lasts only with continued ownership, monitoring, and reinforcement, the "Reinforcement" step in change models such as ADKAR.
Launch events, hidden metrics, and bigger initial budgets don't replace accountability after launch.
4. Business Readiness, Leadership, and AI Transformation

Which TWO statements best describe an organization that has truly achieved enterprise AI transformation? Pick the pair of correct statements.  (1) It runs the largest number of AI pilots in its industry.  (2) Every employee has been told to use AI daily, regardless of fit.  (3) AI is embedded in core processes and decisions, with measurable business value tracked and reported continuously.  (4) A single team builds all AI for the company.  (5) Governance, skills, data foundations, and a culture of continuous improvement let it adopt new AI opportunities quickly and responsibly.
Transformation means AI is part of how the business runs and creates value, supported by lasting capabilities: governance, skills, data, and culture.
Pilot counts, blanket mandates, and a single central build team are signs of activity or bottlenecks, not transformation.
